passages.t: ‘Bless the LORD, O my soul’: do not forget
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “Of David” (verse 1). The psalm opens with a man talking to himself. “Bless the LORD, O my soul; all that is within me, bless His holy name” (verse 1). He says it again: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds” (verse 2).

Then he lists those kind deeds. God is the one “who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases” (verse 3), “who redeems your life from the Pit and crowns you with loving devotion and compassion” (verse 4), “who satisfies you with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
To ‘bless’ God, in the Bible, means to praise him and speak well of him with thanks. Here a man tells his own soul to do it. The soul, nephesh in Hebrew, is not a ghostly part of a person. The book page explains it as the whole living self. ‘All that is within me’ means every part of him.

Why does he need to tell himself? Because people forget. Israel was warned again and again not to forget what God had done. Gratitude does not always come on its own. Sometimes you have to call it up.

The eagle (the Hebrew word covers large birds of prey) was a picture of strength. Many commentators suggest the picture comes from the way such birds seem renewed when they grow new feathers. The ‘Pit’ (verse 4) is the grave, the place of the dead.
passages.later:
Isaiah uses the same bird: “those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31).

The Gospels show Jesus doing what verse 3 says, forgiving sins and healing the sick. Matthew writes that he “healed all the sick”, so that Isaiah's word was fulfilled: “He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases” (Matthew 8:16-17).
passages.hard:
Verse 3 says God ‘heals all your diseases’. What about faithful people who are not healed? It is not a promise that every illness is healed now. The same psalm says plainly that our days are like grass and pass away (verses 15 to 16). Many believers have prayed for healing that did not come, and they did not pray wrong.

Readers take verse 3 in more than one way. Some hear a man thanking God for one real recovery, and turning it into praise. Others see every kind of healing, through rest, through medicine, through doctors and nurses, as God's gift. Christians also read it in the light of the resurrection, when every disease will be healed for good. What the psalm does not allow is the idea that illness means God has stopped loving you.

So if you are ill, this verse is no reason to refuse medical care, and no reason to think your faith has failed. Please keep seeing your doctor, and tell someone you trust how you are. If the weight of illness is too heavy, the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Try the psalm's habit today. Talk to your own soul. Tell yourself to remember. Then name, one by one, what God has done: forgiveness, help, rescue, good things.

Gratitude is often not a feeling first. It is a choice to remember. Feelings may follow.

passages.t: ‘As far as the east is from the west’, ‘As a father has compassion’
passages.happening:
Now the psalm turns from one man's blessings to who God is. “The LORD executes righteousness and justice for all the oppressed” (verse 6). “He made known His ways to Moses” (verse 7).

Then it quotes what God said of himself to Moses. “The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (verse 8). “He will not always accuse us, nor harbor His anger forever” (verse 9). “He has not dealt with us according to our sins” (verse 10).

Three pictures follow. The first is height: “For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him” (verse 11). The second is distance: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (verse 12). The third is a family: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him” (verse 13).

And the reason God is so gentle: “For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Verse 8 is close to God's words to Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:6), as the note on Psalm 86 explains. Verse 7 points to that very scene: God showed Moses his ways after the people had made the golden calf. So the psalm's great words about mercy were first spoken just after a great sin.

‘As far as the east is from the west’ is as far as anything can be. You can walk north until you reach the North Pole, and then you are going south. But you can walk east forever and never be going west. Whether or not the psalmist thought of it that way, the picture is of sins taken away with no meeting point between us and them.

‘He knows our frame’ (verse 14) means God knows what we are made of. ‘We are dust’ recalls Genesis, where the first man was made from the dust of the ground. God does not expect from dust what only God could do.
passages.later:
Micah says of God, “You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19). Hebrews quotes God's promise, “For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12).

Jesus told of a son who came home after wasting everything, and “while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). He taught his followers to pray, “Our Father in heaven” (Matthew 6:9).
passages.hard:
Verse 13 makes a claim about God. It says what God is like: he has compassion like a good father's. It is not a claim that every human father is like that.

If your own father did not show you this kind of compassion, or was not there at all, this verse is not asking you to picture him. It is telling you what you should have been shown, and what God is. God's compassion is not limited by the father you had. Another psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10).
passages.asks:
Do you believe your sins are as far from you as the east is from the west? Or do you keep walking back to collect them? Psalm 103 invites you to leave them where God put them.

And let verse 14 soften the way you treat yourself and others. God remembers that we are dust. Can you be as patient with your own weakness, and with the weakness of the people around you, as he is?

passages.t: ‘His days are like grass’, ‘Bless the LORD, all His works’
passages.happening:
Now the psalm looks at how short a life is. “As for man, his days are like grass” (verse 15). He blooms like a wild flower, “when the wind passes over, it vanishes, and its place remembers it no more” (verse 16).

“But from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends to those who fear Him” (verse 17), the psalm says, and his righteousness to their children's children. Our lives are short. God's love is not.

Then the psalm grows wider and wider. “The LORD has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all” (verse 19). It calls the angels to bless him (verse 20), then all his heavenly hosts (verse 21), then all his works everywhere (verse 22).

And it ends where it began, with one person. “Bless the LORD, O my soul” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Grass and wild flowers in Israel sprang up after the winter rains and were gone within days when the hot wind blew. Psalm 90, a few psalms before, used the same picture. The grass in Psalm 103 is not there to frighten. It is there to make God's love look even longer by contrast.

‘Children's children’ (verse 17) mattered greatly to the first hearers. A family line carried a person's name and life forward. The psalm promises that God's faithfulness will reach generations a person will never meet.

Notice the shape of the whole psalm. It starts with one soul, widens to God's people, then to angels and all creation, and then comes back to one soul. Your small voice is part of a very large choir.
passages.later:
Peter quotes Isaiah: “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever” (1 Peter 1:24-25).

In Revelation, John hears every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea singing, “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever” (Revelation 5:13).
passages.asks:
Your life is short. Psalm 103 does not hide that. But it sets your short life inside a love that runs ‘from everlasting to everlasting’, and reaches to your children's children.

End today the way this psalm ends. Whatever the day was like, say to yourself: ‘Bless the LORD, O my soul.’ You are joining angels when you do.
